articles.title: Bihar now known for development, not scams or crime, says PM Modi
articles.summary: Patna: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday inaugurated several projects worth more than Rs 34,000 crore in Bihar's Vaishali district, including a 19.7 km long bridge on Ganga, which has been named as Nitish Setu. "Naming the bridge as Nitish Setu is a fitting tribute to former Chief Minister Nitish Kumar who established in the rule of law in Bihar and put the State on the fast track of development in the last 20 years. Before NDA rule, Bihar was known for scams and crimes. Now the State is known for development. Nitish ji made rapid progress in terms of infra projects, road connectivity and power sector. Now Samrat Choudhary, the BJP first CM in Bihar, is taking forward the development work initiated by Nitish," said the Prime Minister. Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurates 'Nitish Setu' in Bihar; Opposition says 'self-aggrandisement' Modi was addressing a rally at Jafarpatti in Vaishali, 50 kms from Patna, after inaugurating the Nitish Setu. The rally venue fell under Hajipur, represented by LJP (R) and Union Minister Chirag Paswan. Modi took the occasion to highlight Chirag's father late Ram Vilas Paswan's contributions too and highlighted how development-oriented Ram Vilas Paswan was. The Nitish Setu connects Patna on the southern side of Ganga with Biddupur in Vaishali on the northern side. Incidentally, Biddupur comes under Raghopur Assembly constituency represented by Leader of the Opposition Tejashwi Yadav. Tejashwi asked Modi why he was inaugurating a bridge which was already inaugurated by Nitish Kumar 17 months back and vehicles have been running on the bridge since July 2025. "Is this because you want a plaque in your name on the bridge for which the Central Government headed by you made zero contribution. This 5,000 crore bridge has been built with Rs 3,000 crore assistance given by Asian Development Bank (ADB), besides State government contributing Rs 2,000 crore from its own financial pool," Tejashwi put the record straight. Earlier, Nitish Kumar hugged Modi while welcoming the Prime Minister at the Patna Airport. After inaugurating the bridge, Modi walked on it for a few minutes before waving his 'gamcha' (small towel) towards the crowd.

articles.summary: New Delhi: Grand Theft Auto VI has grossed USD 3.79 billion in day-one retail sales, clinching a new record and becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history, Rockstar Games, a label of Take-Two Interactive Software, has said. Grand Theft Auto VI earned a near-perfect score of 99 on Metacritic, a website that combines professional critics' reviews into a single score out of 100, and drew resounding critical acclaim. It also sold 32.5 million units before release, a new record across all platforms, according to a statement. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world, and we couldn't be more excited to share this moment with you," Sam Houser, President and Founder of Rockstar Games, said. Grand Theft Auto VI is available at the PlayStation Store, Microsoft Store, Rockstar Games Store, and global retailers and storefronts. The latest instalment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise brings eager fans back to the fictional Vice City in a sprawling, immersive virtual adventure. Set in the fictional American state of Leonida, inspired by Florida, GTA VI follows protagonists Jason and Lucia as the pair are pulled into a conspiracy when what looks like an easy score goes wrong. In the US, the GTA VI mania spilled into workplaces this week, with nearly one in five salaried workers - according to a survey - planning to take launch day off. Fans were clearing their work schedules and excusing themselves from meetings to indulge in marathon gaming sessions. In India, both console stores list the Standard Edition at Rs 5,999 and the Ultimate Edition at Rs 7,499. The Ultimate Edition includes extra vehicles, weapons, apparel and other exclusive in-game content.

Ladakh votes after eight years as debate over political representation remains unresolved
articles.summary: Srinagar: More than seven years after Ladakh was separated from Jammu and Kashmir and made a Union Territory, voters on Saturday turned out to elect representatives to municipal and panchayat bodies, amid an unresolved debate over its political future. The elections, the first to these local bodies since Ladakh became a Union Territory in August 2019, are being held after an eight-year gap. The previous panchayat and municipal elections were conducted in 2018, when Ladakh was part of the erstwhile Jammu and Kashmir state. The exercise is significant for a region that has been seeking a greater say in its administration, with the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) leading demands for statehood, constitutional safeguards and protection of land, employment and cultural identity. Unlike several other Union Territories, Ladakh does not have a legislative assembly. Its administration is headed by a Lieutenant Governor, while the two Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (LAHDCs), panchayats and municipal bodies provide different layers of elected local representation. However, the existing arrangements have not addressed the larger political demands being pursued by the region’s civil society groups. Polling began at 8 am in the municipal committees of Leh and Kargil and panchayat constituencies across Ladakh’s eight districts. Voting is scheduled to conclude at 5 pm. According to official figures reported by the Ladakh administration, municipal polling recorded a turnout of 26 per cent till noon, with Kargil registering 44 per cent and Leh 19.8 per cent. Centre offers HPC talks after Ladakh hill council polls, says LAB chairman Lakruk In the panchayat elections, turnout stood at 44.36 per cent in sarpanch constituencies and 48.21 per cent in panch constituencies till noon. The election, however, is being contested in only a portion of the notified grassroots seats, with several candidates elected unopposed. Of the 192 panchayat halqas, 55 sarpanches have been elected unopposed, leaving 137 constituencies for polling. Similarly, 1,186 candidates have been elected unopposed for panch positions out of 1,428, leaving 242 seats for voting. In the municipal elections, all 21 wards of Leh are going to polls, while candidates in four of Kargil’s 17 wards have been elected unopposed. The timing of the elections has also become a point of contention. The LAB and KDA have questioned holding the electoral exercises during winter, arguing that seasonal migration takes a substantial section of the population outside Ladakh and could affect participation. The two organisations have also been pressing the Centre for a broader political arrangement that provides elected representatives with meaningful executive, legislative and financial powers. Their negotiations with the Union Home Ministry have remained deadlocked over the nature and authority of the proposed arrangement. The Centre has explored the possibility of a Union Territory-level elected body, but Ladakh’s political groups have maintained that their demands for statehood and constitutional safeguards must be addressed. The elections are being held ahead of another major political exercise on December 4, when voters will elect representatives to the eight Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils, covering 100 constituencies. For the first time, 36 of these seats have been reserved for women.

articles.title: How this Hyderabad doctor got drug price slashed from Rs 9 crore to Rs 2.5 lakh for seven Indian patients
articles.summary: A Hyderabad-based pediatrician Dr Sivaranjani Santosh has pulled out all the stops in helping seven Indian families get treatment for an extremely rare illness Allan–Herndon–Dudley syndrome (AHDS) that affects physical and mental development. As per records, the commercial cost of the drug treating this condition is nearly rupees 9 crores for people in the United States who may buy it without any insurance cover. Dr Sivaranjani and her associates have raised money in India to pay for a more affordable treatment package , costing up to rupees 2.5 lakhs annually for every child. In a cross-border humanitarian effort, she joined hands with Access to Medicines India, a patient rights group, Organization for Rare Diseases India (ORDI) and Netherlands-based Pharmaceutical Accountability Foundation (PAF) to arrange a medicine treating Allan–Herndon–Dudley syndrome (AHDS) for Indian patients at an affordable cost. Drug price drop is a new lifeline India cannot afford the treatment Egetis Therapeutics AB , a pharmaceutical company which dominates the production of orphan or rare drugs in Sweden and the world, holds a patent right on a drug branded as Emcitate with its active ingredient being tiratricol , an important salt that can help with symptoms of AHDS. In India, there is no treatment for this condition and the heavy import price makes it nearly impossible for consumption by most patients. The only hope for them to date has been to procure the medicine on grounds of compassion. Have not slept well seeing my kid sick Surendra Kumar, a mechanical engineer based in Hyderabad, knew intuitively his two months old baby was not doing well. “I could feel something unusual about my child not being able to focus or listen to sounds. Even the way he tried balancing his head, it felt off. Many people around me, including some doctors, called me overly anxious and obsessed about developmental goals. I just knew something was not adding up even though there was no evidence to prove it,” said Kumar, suggesting the difficulty to spot developmental errors in early infancy. What started off as routine bloodwork for their baby in March 2025 soon brought Kumar to take up more serious tests for him — MRI and then genetic tests. The MRI scan revealed ‘mild demyelination’ (poor insulation around nerves) around nerves tissue, indicative of a developmental problem. One step ahead, a genetic test showed his baby had a very rare X chromosome linked disorder, called the Allan–Herndon–Dudley syndrome (AHDS) or MCT8 deficiency . On finding no available treatment for the rare condition in India, Kumar’s heart skipped a beat and revived with a bleak hope, “There is just one hospital in Mumbai which gives these medicines on humanitarian grounds.” By the time Kumar could gather funds for the travel, the hospital notified him the supply was untimely stopped. With an annual income of rupees 5.5 lakhs, Kumar was eyeing a drug which would cost him nearly rupees 10 lakhs per month. Seven more families Kumar’s case is not the only isolated diagnosis. During a joint effort to bring in a rare medication to Indian households, Dr Sivaranjani and her associates discovered about six children who were having the same medical condition. While one parent directly visited the pediatrician at her clinic in Hyderabad, five other children had been identified at the Christian Medical College (CMC) (Vellore), making the count grow to six. With Dr Sivaranjani using social media as a platform for awareness, even Kumar got attached to the same cause. “The numbers are slowly increasing,” Dr Sivaranjani told Deccan Herald. When Pavitra Sirolkar, mother to a child having AHDS, procured rupees 12 to 13 lakhs for just one month of medicine supply, Dr Sivaranjani knew the treatment plan would not be feasible for most Indian patients. On September 7, Dr Sivaranjani made an appeal on social media and reached out to journalists to amplify her cause and help her get tiratricol for Indian children. She also tagged the Prime Minister, Union Health Minister and other government authorities for their assistance. Meanwhile, an article by FirstPost got the attention of Pharmaceutical Accountability Foundation (PAF), a Netherlands based company who decided to explore the possibility of making a similar medicine using the active ingredient, the raw material which is not patented. Dramatic cost cutting While Egetis Therapeutics AB holds patent for Emcitate , it does not cover the active ingredient Tiratricol as it is not a newly discovered or man-made molecule but an established thyroid hormone metabolite. Hence, the patent is only limited to compound formulation of the branded drug. This enabled Transvaal pharmacy (in Netherland) to undertake the test batches and make formulations for seven children. According to PAF, the total cost of making these formulations came to a figure of rupees 15.08 lakhs. Out of which, rupees 6.09 lakhs have been raised by Dr Sivaranjani and her associates and the remaining rupees 9.13 lakhs will be raised by the PAF. For a treatment which can cost up to crores, it will be delivered to Indian children for almost free. Allan–Herndon–Dudley syndrome (AHDS) AHDS is a serious but extremely rare genetic disorder associated with X chromosome, usually affecting male children who inherit the faulty gene from the mother. It causes severe developmental delay and limits thyroid signaling in the brain, resulting in late myelination (protective, insulating layer around the nerve fibers), poor reception of hormone activity, impaired differentiation of white and grey matter and in some cases, loss of brain volume. The children affected by the condition often don’t reach developmental milestones and become wheelchair bound by adulthood, experts have said. In this condition, the brain of the child gets starved of thyroid stimulation and levels of circulating triiodothyronine (T3) gets elevated in the blood, slowly getting absorbed by muscles, heart and liver. A state called thyrotoxicosis happens when there is too much thyroid hormone in the body and poor reception of it in the brain. “Tiratricol binds with thyroid receptors in the brain and helps bring down levels of T3 in the blood, thus improving metabolic symptoms and pushing development, particularly in growing children. The earlier a person begins the treatment, the better will be the results,” said Dr Sivaranjani. “She appeared as a Goddess” When DH asked Kumar on the drug availability and dramatic cost cut, he said: “For us parents, Dr Sivaranjani has been a Goddess who gave us hope that our children can have a normal life. She is a healer in the truest sense.” “As a father, I just want to see my son able to sit on his own and move around his head to hear voices or see things around. For now, this is all we want, a big smile on his face. I have not slept well in months, thinking my son is in so much pain and misery," he added. The pediatrician had also run a successful campaign against sugary drinks getting passed with an ‘ORS’ label, pressuring FSSAI to limit the label to only formulations meeting standards set by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2025. When DH asked Dr Sivaranjani on how she plans to help more children affected by this condition, she said: “It is just the first step of the ladder. Now, we will work towards making domestic production of tiratricol possible in India. If other labs can make it, why can't we.”

articles.title: 14-year-old hacker held for trying to sell private data of 4,000 Agniveers on dark web: Delhi Police
articles.summary: New Delhi: A 14-year-old boy from Haryana's Ballabhgarh was apprehended by the Delhi Police Special Cell for allegedly hacking into a website and attempting to sell sensitive data linked to around 4,000 Agniveer personnel on the dark web for USD 500, officials said. According to investigators, the juvenile gained unauthorised access to a test website designed for former Agniveers to register themselves and explore employment opportunities in other government departments. After accessing the website, the boy allegedly extracted the information and posted an advertisement on the dark web, claiming to possess personal data of around 4,000 Agniveers and offering to sell it for USD 500, they said. Investigation has revealed that artificial intelligence tools were allegedly used to access the information, officials said, adding that the exact method employed to breach the website is being examined. The Delhi Police's Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit has recovered data from the juvenile's digital devices. Investigators are now examining the material to ascertain whether it contains genuine information and establish the extent of the suspected breach. Guidelines issued during anti-CEC protest to distinguish journalists from reel-makers, Delhi police tell Supreme Court The police have also written to the Union Ministry of Home Affairs seeking the official database of Agniveers to match it with the recovered information and verify its authenticity. The juvenile was apprehended and questioned in accordance with the law. Following preliminary questioning, he was handed over to his family, officials said. Further investigation is underway to determine how the website was accessed, whether the information was compromised beyond the data recovered from the boy's devices and if any third party had purchased or accessed the purported database. The incident has brought the security of digital platforms containing information related to Agniveer personnel under scrutiny, even as investigators work to establish the nature and scale of the alleged data breach. The Centre launched the Agnipath recruitment scheme in June 2022 to induct personnel into the Army, Navy and Air Force for a four-year tenure. Those recruited under the scheme, known as Agniveers, undergo military training before being deployed in their respective services.

articles.summary: New Delhi: Adani Defence & Aerospace, the Adani Group's flagship defence and aerospace company, successfully demonstrated Bagheera AT1, a vehicle-mounted anti-tank guided missile (ATGM) system, at the Pokhran Field Firing Ranges in Rajasthan. "The programme validated day and night engagements, a two-missile tandem firing along a single beam against a target representing an armoured vehicle, and an aerial-target engagement at an extended range. It was followed by a static display of the complete system," the company said in a statement. The No Cost No Commitment (NCNC) demonstration at Pokhran on November 20 was witnessed by senior representatives of the Indian Army, Department of Military Affairs and Ministry of Defence (MoD). "Bagheera AT1 is the outcome of 18 months of design and development, during which Adani Defence customised the missile system for Indian terrain, climate and operational requirements. The result is a complete combat system comprising the missile, automated launcher, day and night sights, mounted on an Adani Defence- designed 4x4 high-mobility armoured vehicle," it said. HCL's Shiv Nadar most generous Indian; Gautam Adani doubles donations, Mukesh Ambani's support down 1%: Report The missile is capable of engaging armour at up to 8 km, twice the approximately 4 km range of the land-based anti-tank missile. It rides a laser beam rather than relying on a radio link, making it highly resistant to electronic jamming on a battlefield increasingly shaped by drones and electronic warfare. The company said two missiles can be fired in quick succession along the same beam at a single target. "The first engages the tank's Active Protection System (APS), while the second is designed to penetrate its defences." Four ready-to-fire missiles on the automated launcher and 8 reloads onboard, providing a total capacity of 12 missiles per vehicle. Also, integrated day television and thermal-imaging sights with automated target tracking. The crew engages from cover and relocates quickly to reduce exposure to enemy fire. "The system can also engage aerial targets at extended range," the statement said. India's requirement for modern anti-tank guided missiles remains substantial, with reported gaps in the ATGM inventory underscoring the need for continued modernisation. The in-service backbone remains second-generation Milan-2T and Konkurs-M, with Spike missiles subsequently inducted to address immediate operational requirements. India is also progressing with the acquisition of Javelin systems. "Recent conflicts have underscored the importance of range and mobility in armoured engagements. Bagheera AT1 offers the Army an additional long-range, mobile ground capability alongside man-portable and helicopter-launched missiles," the firm said. India's defence production reached a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in FY 2025-26. The private sector's share rose to 24 per cent, or about Rs 42,000 crore, from 22 per cent a year earlier, while defence exports hit a record Rs 38,424 crore. "Bagheera AT1 demonstrates the growing role of India's private sector in developing, integrating and delivering advanced defence systems tailored to the operational requirements of Armed Forces. Adani Defence & Aerospace has undertaken the development, integration and testing of a complete combat system, providing the Armed Forces with a system for evaluation," it added. Adani Defence & Aerospace, part of the Adani Group, is India's largest integrated private defence and aerospace company, building critical capabilities across land, air and sea.

articles.title: Kerala HC allows RSS-linked teachers' body to hold exam in state schools
articles.summary: The Kerala High Court on Friday, November 20, permitted a teachers’ organisation affiliated with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) to conduct its district-level Young Scholar Exam 2026 in government and aided schools across the state on November 22. The interim order comes despite the state government withdrawing its earlier permission for the examination, following allegations that it could be used to propagate Hindu nationalist ideology among schoolchildren. The examination is being organised by the National Teachers’ Union (NTU), Kerala, the state unit of the Akhil Bharatiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh (ABRSM), a teachers’ organisation associated with the Sangh Parivar. It is being conducted in association with Mayilpeeli, a children's magazine published by Balagokulam, an organisation linked to the RSS and known for organising Sree Krishna Jayanti celebrations in Kerala. The involvement of these organisations triggered a political controversy after the General Education Department initially permitted the examination to be conducted in government and aided schools. Justice Gopinath P issued the interim order on a petition filed by T Anoop Kumar, general secretary of Deshiya Adhyapaka Parishath (NTU) Kerala, challenging the General Education Department's November 14 order withdrawing the permission granted earlier. While allowing the examination to proceed as scheduled, the court restrained the organisers from publishing its results or conducting any further examinations without obtaining additional orders from the court. “Since all arrangements have been made for conduct of the examination on 22.11.2026, there will be an interim order directing that the petitioner shall be permitted to conduct the examination,” the court said. The order further clarified: “The petitioner/the organization conducting the examination shall not declare any results of the examination and shall not conduct any further examination, without obtaining further orders from this Court.” The dispute arose after the Director of General Education granted permission to NTU on October 12 to conduct the Young Scholar Exam 2026 for students from Classes 5 to 10 in government and aided schools. The approval was subsequently withdrawn following complaints and political criticism, with General Education Minister N Samsudheen directing the department to revoke the permission. During Friday’s hearing, the Additional Advocate General, appearing for the state government, submitted that the permission granted to the petitioner had been issued by mistake. The government maintained that organisations affiliated with political parties and religious organisations could not be permitted to conduct such examinations in state schools. The petitioner's counsel, however, argued that the November 14 order withdrawing the permission did not state any reasons for the decision. The counsel also submitted that the organisers had not been given an opportunity to be heard before the permission was revoked. Further, the examination was scheduled for November 22, and all arrangements had already been completed, the court was told. After hearing both sides, the court admitted the writ petition and issued the interim direction allowing the examination to go ahead, subject to the restrictions on declaring results and holding further examinations. The case has been posted for further consideration on December 10. The original approval had drawn strong criticism from the Students Federation of India (SFI) and the Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)], which questioned the government's decision to allow an RSS-linked organisation to conduct an examination in state schools. Actor Unni Mukundan had also been named the brand ambassador of the scholarship examination.

articles.title: Accident can’t be termed self-inflicted to deny war injury pension: Supreme Court
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Supreme Court has ruled that an officially recorded accident involving a service weapon cannot be converted into a self-inflicted injury to deny war injury pension to an Army personnel. A bench of Justices Satish Chandra Sharma and N Kotiswar Singh allowed the appeal of Ex-Subedar Major and Honorary Lieutenant Devi Singh and directed the Union government to grant him the War Injury Element of pension from the date of his retirement on March 31, 2019. High time MoD frames clear rules on Army service conditions,' SC upholds war injury pension to Army veteran The court set aside the Armed Forces Tribunal (Lucknow) order of May 10, 2023, which had rejected the claim mainly because the Adjutant General’s branch had not issued a final battle casualty certificate. Devi Singh sustained a gunshot wound on August 7, 2002, while serving in Jammu and Kashmir during Operation Rakshak/Operation Parakram. His loaded weapon accidentally discharged, the bullet passing through his left thigh and damaging the femoral vein. Contemporaneous records established it as a battle accident on duty. The medical board assessed 40% permanent disability attributable to service. The court rejected the Centre’s stand that accidental discharge of one’s own weapon fell short of the operational threshold. “The distinction pertinent to note here is that the exclusion is of a self-inflicted injury injury, not of every injury in which a serviceman’s own weapon happens to be the source of the bullet... Weapon ownership and intention are distinct facts,” the bench pointed out in its judgment on November 20, 2026. The bench held that in the absence of contrary contemporaneous material, an officially recorded accident cannot be converted into a self-inflicted injury merely because the weapon belonged to the appellant. The court declared the disability fell within “action against extremists or anti-social elements.” Both parameters under Army Order 1/2003/MP—accidental gunshot wound during operations and grievous nature—were satisfied. Relying on Union of India Vs Saroj Devi (2024), it said official contemporaneous certificates must be given due evidentiary weight. The court also opined absence of the name from a later digital database or destruction of files in the 2014 floods could not disprove surviving records. “The appellant, therefore, cannot be made to suffer for no fault on his part,” the bench held, directing sanction of war injury element within three months, adjusting the disability pension already paid.

articles.title: In last 12 years, India has shown it can break limits, unlock possibilities: PM Modi
articles.summary: Kharagpur (WB): Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday said India has demonstrated in the last 12 years that breaking barriers in mindset could unlock the country's potential, create opportunities and empower the poor, while asserting that he believed in challenging challenges rather than allowing limitations to hold the nation back. Addressing the platinum jubilee celebrations of IIT Kharagpur, the country's first Indian Institute of Technology, Modi said the next two decades would be crucial for realising the 'Viksit Bharat' vision, asserting that India had declared "loud and clear" its resolve to "break the limits and unlock the possibilities". "Our strength is determined by how courageously we dare to challenge challenges. People often ask me about challenges. I tell them that it is in my very nature that I cannot rest without challenging a challenge," he said, adding that people often imposed limitations on themselves. "Nations recognise their true capabilities only when they break the limitations of their thinking. India has demonstrated precisely this over the past few years. India has declared with confidence: break the limits, unlock the possibilities. Over the past few years, India has shown this," he said. PM Modi reaches rally venue in Bihar's Vaishali swirling 'gamcha' atop open vehicle The prime minister said his government had worked over the last 12 years to change the prevailing mindset about poverty and empower people through various initiatives. Recalling that poverty was once considered an insurmountable challenge, Modi said successive governments had raised slogans about eradicating it, but the administration had failed to act because of a belief that poverty could not be eliminated in a country with such a large population. "Until 20 years ago, poverty was considered a permanent problem in our country. Five decades ago, slogans about eradicating poverty were raised from the ramparts of the Red Fort. Yet, whenever it came to taking action at the policy level, the entire system would simply bury the matter in files," he said. Modi also recalled facing ridicule in Parliament when he announced from the Red Fort that his government would construct toilets for the poor. "When I announced from the Red Fort that I would build toilets for the poor, people in Parliament made fun of me... Such people could not understand how important a toilet was for a poor family, particularly for poor women," he said. In the last 12 years, the central government sought to change this mindset, he said, adding that he believed in the principle of "power to empower". Citing a World Bank report, Modi claimed that around 50 crore people had been brought out of poverty in India in the last 12-13 years, describing it as the outcome of a mindset that believed in breaking limitations. "This is no small achievement. It is the result of a mindset that believes in breaking the limits," he said. Emphasising the importance of putting national interests first, Modi urged students to follow the mantra of "nation first", saying it would create new opportunities for them while contributing to the country's development. "Nation first... When you move forward with this mindset, it will certainly bring new opportunities for you as well, and the country will also benefit greatly," he said. He asked students and faculty members of IIT Kharagpur to resolve to work towards making India a developed nation in the next 20 years. "By 2047, many of you will be in leadership roles... In the 2018 state assembly elections, the Congress had secured a majority by a narrow margin and returned to power after 15 years. The party's then state president Kamal Nath was made the chief minister in December 2018. Union minister Hardeep Puri declared elected unopposed to Rajya Sabha from Madhya Pradesh However, in March 2020, Scindia raised the flag of rebellion and joined the BJP along with his 22 supporting MLAs, including six ministers. The development led to the collapse of the 15-month-old Kamal Nath-led Congress government in the state. Nath had to resign from the chief minister's post. "Things deteriorated after open verbal spats like 'I will see on the street' took place among the senior leaders," he claimed. Amid the bitterness prevailing at that time, Scindia had said that if promises made in the election manifesto were not fulfilled, he would hit the streets against his own party's government, to which Kamal Nath had bluntly replied, "Toh utar jayein sadak par (Let him take to the streets)." articles.title: Padmaja Venugopal apologises to Congress workers, says she wants to rejoin party
articles.summary: Padmaja Venugopal, daughter of former Kerala chief minister and Congress veteran K Karunakaran, has apologised to Congress workers for joining the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in 2024. The apology comes amid growing opposition within the Congress to her proposed return to the party following her exit from the BJP on November 19. In a Facebook post on Saturday, November 21, Padmaja said she had realised that her decision to join the BJP had deeply hurt Congress workers who were fond of both her and her father. She said she was preparing to return after recognising the impact her departure had on the party and its workers. “When I said, while resigning, that joining the BJP was a wrong decision I had made in an emotional moment, I was speaking from my heart. I realised that the decision I had taken back then deeply hurt many Congress workers who loved both K Karunakaran and me. It was this realisation that prompted me to prepare for a return,” she said. Stating that she was not aspiring for any position within the party, Padmaja said her only wish was to become a Congress worker again. She also acknowledged the criticism directed at her by Congress workers from different parts of the state and apologised for the hurt caused by her decision. “I fully acknowledge and accept the criticism levelled against me by Congress workers from various quarters. I would also like to use this opportunity to sincerely apologise, from the bottom of my heart, to every Congress worker and to the party for the hurt my decision caused,” she said. Padmaja added that her immediate aim was to pay her respects at her father's memorial alongside Congress workers on his death anniversary next month. Her statement comes a day after reports emerged that she had contacted Kerala Pradesh Congress Committee (KPCC) president Sunny Joseph and expressed her wish to return to the party. Sunny confirmed the phone conversation but said the Congress had not received a formal request from her. He said the matter had not been discussed at the party level and that a decision would be taken after consultations with the leadership. Her proposed return has, however, triggered opposition from sections of the Congress, particularly younger leaders who have questioned whether she has adequately addressed the political positions she took against the party before joining the BJP. Congress spokesperson Jinto John said Padmaja should first demonstrate political clarity regarding her stance on the Sangh Parivar's ideology before seeking readmission to the party. In a strongly worded response, he said she should return without conditions, as an ordinary worker or supporter, and not expect preferential treatment because of her family background. Jinto listed several questions concerning her earlier statements, including her allegations of sexism within the Congress, her remarks about Congress leaders, her criticism of Shafi Parambil, and her support for the film The Kerala Story . He also questioned her continued positive assessment of Prime Minister Narendra Modi after quitting the BJP. He said Padmaja had not yet explicitly rejected the BJP's politics or the Sangh Parivar's ideology and that leaving the party for personal reasons was not sufficient. “Before stepping through the open doorway, there are certain political issues that need to be corrected. All of these must be sincerely corrected and stated loudly,” he said. Jinto also argued that Congress workers who had remained with the party despite her departure should not have their commitment and self-respect undermined by an easy return for those who had switched political loyalties. He said Padmaja's family legacy could not automatically guarantee her acceptance within the party. Congress student wing Kerala Students Union (KSU) president Aloysious Xavier also opposed any preferential treatment for Padmaja. Referring to the possible return of Padmaja and former BJP leader Padmini Thomas, he described it as a season of 'ghar wapsi' (homecoming). In a social media post, Aloysious said thousands of Congress workers had taken to the streets and fought ideological battles, not for individuals who switched political loyalties. He said those returning should work at the booth level and that ordinary workers who had worked for the party for years should be considered for organisational positions. Leaders of the Mahila Congress have also reportedly expressed reservations about Padmaja's re-entry. A Mahila Congress leader said several women had worked hard for the organisation for years, while there were now discussions about welcoming back those who had left for the BJP, allegedly in pursuit of positions. However, some senior Congress leaders have favoured facilitating her return. Thiruvananthapuram District Congress Committee president N Shaktan said the party had a tradition of welcoming people back, while maintaining that her decision to join the BJP could not be justified simply because she was K Karunakaran's daughter. A KPCC office-bearer also indicated that the leadership could respond positively if Padmaja formally approached the party. The final decision, however, would be taken after discussions with Chief Minister VD Satheesan and senior Congress leaders Ramesh Chennithala and KC Venugopal, the office-bearer said. Padmaja's brother and Health Minister K Muraleedharan declined to comment on her possible return, saying the KPCC president and the Chief Minister would take a call. He said he did not wish to express a personal opinion on any individual, though he welcomed people joining the Congress from the BJP. Padmaja quit the BJP on November 19, nearly two years after leaving the Congress in March 2024, ahead of the Lok Sabha elections. At the time, she had accused sections of the Congress leadership of sidelining and insulting her, particularly in Thrissur, and alleged that the party's culture was hostile to women. She subsequently joined the BJP and contested the 2026 Assembly election from Thrissur, finishing third. Announcing her exit from the BJP, Padmaja described her decision to join the party as a mistake made in haste and in an emotional moment. She said she had no complaints against BJP leaders but found it difficult to reconcile her Congress family background and ideological inheritance with the party's politics. She had also said that Prime Minister Narendra Modi had done several good things but had made mistakes too, adding that she could not point them out while she was in the BJP. At the time of her exit, Padmaja said she had not taken a decision on returning to the Congress and wanted to carry forward programmes associated with her father. She had said she had discussed her decision to quit the BJP with her brother Muraleedharan, who advised her to do what would give her peace and happiness.

The former chief minister said students work hard their entire lives, and should be provided free and fair examinations. "If we cannot even provide the children with a free and fair examination, where they can achieve something in life based on their own capability, their own hard work, and their own merit; if we cannot even give them that, then what will we give them? Then our children will go into depression," she said. Mehbooba alleged that scams have been happening repeatedly and lamented that the situation remained the same despite an elected government at the helm. articles.summary: Amritsar: Punjab MP and Akali Dal Waris Punjab De chief Amritpal Singh on Saturday arrived at his residence in Jallupur Khera village where he met his family members after he was flown to Amritsar from New Delhi under tight security arrangements. A court in Amritsar has granted him permission to attend his grandmother's cremation at his native village, Jallupur Khera, in Amritsar. On Friday, the MP was brought from Assam's Dibrugarh jail to Delhi. Videos and pictures appeared on social media showing the Khadoor Sahib MP entering his residence with folded hands. In a video, Singh could be seen embracing one of his relatives. Only select family members were allowed to meet Singh who was brought from the Amritsar airport to his village, Jallupur Khera, in a convoy of police vehicles. Police personnel have been deployed at his residence. Later, Singh took part in a funeral procession from the residence in a tractor trolley for the final rites of his grandmother. He was accompanied by his family members and Waris Punjab De leaders. Jailed MP Amritpal Singh to attend grandmother's cremation under tight security on Nov 21 A five-member Punjab Police team on Friday took custody of the 33-year-old MP. Singh returns to Punjab after more than three and a half years, which he has spent in a Dibrugarh jail in connection with an attack on a police station. The court on Tuesday granted Singh permission to attend the cremation for three hours on November 21. It directed the Punjab government to ensure Singh's physical presence at Jallupur Khera village from 12 noon to 3 pm on Saturday, subject to conditions laid down in its November 13 order. Punjab Police have made elaborate security arrangements in and around Jallupur Khera village. Sufficient force has been deployed to maintain law and order, a senior police officer said. Earlier, Akali Dal Waris Punjab De chief spokesperson Shamsher Singh Padhri said Singh will first be taken to his residence and from there he will be brought to the cremation ground. Arrangements have been made on eight acres of land to accommodate a large number of attendees at the cremation. Parking space has been created at four locations, besides arrangements for 'langar' for the gathering. Barricades have been erected around the cremation site to regulate the movement of people. Singh's grandmother, Charan Kaur (84), died on November 8 following prolonged illness. The Khadoor Sahib MP was granted a three-hour permission on November 14, but could not be brought to Punjab as authorities expressed their inability to make arrangements at such short notice. His legal team subsequently moved a fresh plea. Kaur's remains have been kept in Jallupur Khera village, with the family deferring the cremation until Singh could attend the last rites. The family has scheduled the cremation for November 21, the collection of ashes for November 22 and the 'bhog' ceremony for November 23. Singh has been in jail since 2023 in connection with a police station attack case. On February 23, 2023, Singh and his supporters, some of them brandishing swords and guns, stormed Ajnala police station on the outskirts of Amritsar and clashed with police while trying to secure the release of his aides detained there. He was arrested on April 23, 2023, following a month-long manhunt and subsequently detained under the National Security Act (NSA). After his detention under the NSA ended on April 22 this year, he was arrested again on April 23 and lodged in the Dibrugarh jail. Singh contested the 2024 Lok Sabha elections as an independent candidate and won from Khadoor Sahib.

articles.title: Allahabad High Court pulls up Uttar Pradesh government over registration of FIRs under law declared 'stillborn' by top court
articles.summary: Lucknow: The Allahabad High Court's Lucknow Bench has sought an explanation from the state government over registration of FIRs under the Uttar Pradesh Gangsters and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986, despite the Supreme Court having declared the legislation "stillborn". A division bench of Justices Abdul Moin and Pramod Kumar on Friday directed the additional chief secretary (Home) to file a personal affidavit within three weeks explaining why such cases are still being registered. The court warned that in case of non-compliance, the officer would have to appear personally along with the relevant records. The matter has been listed for December 15. "Once the law with regard to the Act has been enunciated by the apex court in August 2026, there cannot be any occasion for the authorities to continue with the registration of FIRs under the provisions of the Act" the bench observed. Azam Khan released from Ghaziabad jail after Allahabad High Court grants interim bail The court also sought details of the action proposed against officials responsible for registering such cases and the corrective measures being taken to prevent recurrence. The bench remarked that it should not be repeatedly required to point out the authorities' failure to comply with Supreme Court judgments. It also expressed concern that litigants were being forced to approach the high court over the issue, resulting in a waste of "precious judicial time of the Constitutional court". The observations came during the hearing of a writ petition filed by Brijesh Kumar alias Banty Verma, challenging an FIR registered on October 23 under Section 3(1) of the Act at Akbarpur police station in Ambedkar Nagar district. The petitioner argued that the Supreme Court, in its August 2026 judgment in Shiv Pratap Singh alias Chinu vs State of Uttar Pradesh and Others, had declared the Uttar Pradesh Gangsters and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986, "stillborn" and, therefore, the authorities could not continue proceedings under it. Taking note of the submissions, the high court stayed the FIR and directed that no further proceedings be undertaken in the matter until further orders. The bench also noted that additional government advocates had earlier brought the continued registration of FIRs under the Act to the authorities' attention, but apparently no action had been taken.

Saying that the bridge had been operational for the last 17 months, he added, "...it’s beyond understanding of people of Bihar that why you are inaugurating it again? Besides, traffic congestion on the over 40-year-old Mahatma Gandhi Setu, connecting Patna and Hajipur, is expected to come down after 'Nitish Setu' becomes operational. It will reduce travel time between north and south Bihar and particularly benefit residents of Raghopur Diara by improving their access to Patna and essential services such as healthcare and education, the officials said. The project will also facilitate the movement of agricultural produce and industrial goods, improve access to markets and promote trade and commerce across the region, contributing to Bihar's economic development, they added.

articles.title: India vs New Zealand | K L Rahul 2.0 loading, the man with a mission
articles.summary: Wellington: As bizarre as it may sound, when K L Rahul strode out to bat in the opening Test against New Zealand on Friday, it was like stepping into the unknown for the most capped player in the playing XI and second most in the squad. Despite playing his 71st game in white flannels for India after having made his debut way back in December 2014 against Australia, this was his first-ever Test in New Zealand. India vs New Zealand | K L Rahul, Shubman Gill put visitors in the driver's seat The 34-year-old was not picked for the two Tests in New Zealand in early 2020 owing to poor form, and not having played here was one glaring lacuna in his largely impressive resume that boasts of centuries at some of cricket’s iconic venues like Sydney Cricket Ground, Lord’s and Centurion. Adding New Zealand, the historical Basin Reserve specifically, to that list had been his top priority over the last few months. That apart, Rahul was also determined to etch his name in history by becoming just the fifth Indian after Mohammad Azharuddin, Sachin Tendulkar, Rahul Dravid and Virat Kohli to score a century in SENA (South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia) countries. Wellington and Christchurch would be his final shot at it. India vs New Zealand | Windy Wellington poses a tough challenge for visitors From the moment he strode to the crease, the reinvigorated Rahul was a man on a mission. Bringing all his experience to the fore and putting into practice the learnings of having watched videos of several former players who’d excelled in New Zealand, Rahul struck a composed 136 off 290 balls to become just the second opener from Asia after Pakistan’s Saeed Anwar to score a century in SENA countries. Speaking to the media after having checked off that one big box, a delighted Rahul said strong preparation is the reason behind the latest success. “When you play Test cricket or when you play cricket for that long, when you finish your career, you want to at least get that opportunity to challenge yourself in different countries and play against the best attacks. And obviously, New Zealand has been a country that a lot of batters have struggled to get runs in and it is difficult conditions. “I wanted to play a Test match here. I wanted to play a lot more. But unfortunately, I haven't played before this. When I got the opportunity, I wanted to make the most of it. That's why I decided to come in early as well just to get used to the conditions because I've no prior experience of coming to New Zealand and playing red-ball cricket.” “I've been thinking about Test cricket in New Zealand for the last six or seven months, trying to do my homework, trying to see the guys that have scored runs here and how they have been able to achieve that. A lot of preparation, a lot of hard, a lot of like homework. So once I got the opportunity, then if I ticked all those boxes, then it becomes slightly easier when you go play the game.” Something which Rahul did exceptionally across two days was leaving the ball, an art that is not appreciated in modern day cricket. Rahul felt it is very crucial for a batter in seaming conditions. “There was a time when I wasn't opening for 15-18 months. I was playing in the middle order. I had a habit of playing bat on ball. But when I went back to opening the batting, that's something that I consciously tried to do. I used to work in nets as well. “Sometimes, less balls on the bat is the best approach in seeming conditions. I worked on that. Over the years, whenever we've gone out to play, I've watched other openers and how they've been successful. Somebody like Alastair Cook. When I played in England, I used to watch him from slips and see how he batted. He left a lot of deliveries. “He made the bowlers bowl at him. It's the basics of cricket. But sometimes, basic things are the most difficult. As I've gotten slightly older, I've worked on that again. It has helped me a lot with opening.” Rahul spoke at length, giving detailed insights on his preparation and how hard he still works to stay on top of his game. No wonder, he is in the class of elite.

articles.title: 'Focus on our soldiers, not AI and VFX': Salman Khan slams online backlash over 'Maatrubhumi: May War Rest in Peace'
articles.summary: Bollywood superstar Salman Khan has reacted strongly at the online backlash surrounding the teaser and trailer of his upcoming war drama, Maatrubhumi: May War Rest in Peace . Speaking to the media during a promotional event in Hyderabad on Friday, the Dabangg star denied the viral claims that his upcoming movie relies too heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) and shoddy VFX, urging audience to look past technical niggling and connect with the emotional journey of the soldiers. LATEST: Salman Khan Blasts People who are trolling Maatrubhumi for AI! #SVC63 Media - Bhai trailer ki trolling hui hai Salman - Acha hai vfx pe dhyan do, army and emotions pe mat do. #SalmanKhan pic.twitter.com/tAjk0gyZH4 — Being ADARSH⚡ (@IBeingAdarsh_) November 20, 2026 After Salman Khan, Shah Rukh Khan steps up to support ailing Sharad Kapoor following viral video appeal Salman Khan wishes 'Eetha' team 'all the best' before 'Maatrubhumi' face-off 'Maatrubhumi' Trailer: Salman Khan leads Indian soldiers against Chinese troops in intense war drama The online criticism began after the teaser and songs and intensified following the release of the nearly five-minute trailer. These promotional assets sparked massive online debate, with many claiming several visuals looked AI-generated and that Salman hadn't even filmed those scenes in person. Visibly upset by these unverified claims, the superstar came down hard on the critics. "We made this film to tell stories about our country's soldiers and their families. Leaving aside those things, you are talking about AI and VFX. Who are these people? Where do they come from? Are they AI specialists? Are they VFX specialists?" Salman asked. Dismissing the green-screen rumours, Salman said that the team filmed on real locations in punishing conditions. Calling the war drama the most physically exhausting project he has ever done, he requested viewers, "When the film releases, I want the audience to focus on the emotions we have put into showing what our soldiers go through. Focus on their pain, their families, and their children. Please do not sit there checking for AI and VFX." He also addressed the negative remarks that the five-minute trailer was long and gave away too much of the plot. Turning the criticism into a tongue-in-cheek compliment, he said that trolls must have rewatched the preview 15 to 20 times to dissect every frame. "Those saying the trailer is too long or thinking that we have shown the whole film, we haven't. I will show you the whole film on December 4. What is it that they say? Never judge a book by its cover? But you have already judged it by its cover," said Salman. #SalmanKhan replied to vfx and AI warriors "AI dhundhne ke liye 5 baar trailer dekha hai to 2.30hr ka movie to 4-5 baar dekhna Banta hi hai" "Aap log bas vfx or AI note Krna Soldier ka sacrifice mat dekhna" #Maatrubhumi pic.twitter.com/19cOH4WyLS — Parlu (@pani_puri20) November 20, 2026 He further added a note of sarcasm toward trolls, saying that if speaking negatively about him or his film helped content creators gain views, followers, or money, he was "more than happy" for them. Directed by Apoorva Lakhia and produced under Salman Khan Films, Maatrubhumi: May War Rest in Peace (previously titled Battle of Galwan ) chronicles the 2020 border clash between Indian troops of the 16 Bihar Regiment and Chinese forces in the Galwan Valley. Starring Salman Khan, Chitrangada Singh, Anoop Bikram Shahi and Prashant Tamang, the film is scheduled to be released in theatres on December 4, 2026.

articles.summary: After earning a degree in economics from Delhi University, advertising at IIMC and completing an MBA from MICA, Srishti Singh landed a corporate job in Singapore. But she left it all to become an actor. She recently made her acting debut playing Darshana opposite Arjun Das in director Madhumita’s thriller John Doe . As her performance gets praise from all quarters, the actress speaks to DH's NP Jayaraman, opening up about quitting her corporate job, learning Tamil from scratch and surprising everyone with her silver-screen debut. ( Edited excerpts ) You grew up in Haryana, studied in Delhi and had a corporate career before entering Tamil cinema with John Doe . How did this shift happen? It has been a long road and I call myself a “late newcomer”. When I was eight, I wanted to be a "heroine”, though doing college theatre in Delhi and workshops with National School of Drama directors made me fall in love with storytelling. Coming from a middle-class family in Haryana, acting wasn’t seen as a safe career. So, I studied economics at DU, went to IIMC and MICA and did a corporate job for about three years. In 2017, while working in Singapore, I knew I didn't belong there. I quit my job over a text and moved to a remote village in Uttarakhand. Working with local schools brought me close to art and by early 2023, I moved to Mumbai to try my luck in acting. How did John Doe and director Madhumita come your way? Staying in touch with old college friends connected me to the Hyderabad-based production house Arka Media Works. Once I saw director Madhumita’s previous work, I was really blown away by her narration. I went through a few rounds of auditions before she felt I fit the "fish out of water" vibe she wanted for Darshana. View this post on Instagram Starting your career by playing a mother isn’t the usual choice for a newcomer. Did you hesitate? Not at all. I never got into acting for the glitz and glamour. I’m very independent and a bit of a rebel, while the character I played (Darshana) is completely focused on her family and dealing with a lot of personal loss. Playing someone opposite to who I am was very challenging. John Doe was shot with live sound on set. How tough was it to act in Tamil? People in Mumbai told me, "Just mumble your lines ; someone else will dub over it later". That felt like cheating to me. Since it was my very first film and they were recording live audio, I wanted my own voice in the movie. As soon as I got the chance, I immediately found a tutor (Madhuri ma’am) and started learning Tamil. I love picking up new languages and even learned Kumaoni when I spent my time in Uttarakhand. In the end, the makers felt my peculiar accent actually made the character feel more real, since Darshana isn't a native Tamil speaker either. What was it like working with Arjun Das and the rest of the team? Working with Arjun Das was great, though I was super nervous at first. He has such a strong voice and great control over his lines, and I didn’t want my basic Tamil to mess up his flow. But he was very kind and went out of his way to make me feel comfortable. I had a blast working with Zaara Vineet - she was a complete sport. Whenever the shoot got delayed in tough locations, we would sit in the caravan and swap stories about Tamil culture and life in North India. View this post on Instagram How did your family and relatives react when the movie came out? Honestly, I didn’t even tell my extended family that I was trying to act. They thought I was working a regular office job in Mumbai. Only a couple of close cousins knew. When John Doe was released, the love I got from everyone really surprised me. Relatives actually travelled from different states to Gurgaon just to watch the movie in theatres with my parents. Now that your first film is out and getting good reviews, what is next for you? Acting in a new language has removed a big mental block for me and I feel like I can pull off anything if I put in the hard work. Right now, I’m reading a few Hindi and regional scripts that I’m genuinely excited about, though I would love to keep working in Tamil cinema if the right projects come along.

articles.title: As Donald Trump basks in summit pomp, China's Xi Jinping strengthens his hand
articles.summary: Bejing: Donald Trump hailed the fanfare of his meeting this week with Xi Jinping as a victory, but the US president has gained little from three such summits this year while the Chinese leader has strengthened his position on the world stage, analysts say. Xi emerged from a global gathering in China as a statesman who could convene the first China-US-Russia summit and he keeps a fragile trade truce with the US in a holding pattern — where Beijing likes it — even as Washington takes a harder line. At least in terms of public announcements, Trump has few concrete gains to show. "They have achieved the Chinese Communist Party's and Xi's goal, which was to keep dragging things out and keep talking," said Kuo Yu-jen, director of Taiwan's National Sun Yat-sen University's Institute of China and Asia-Pacific Studies. 'Look at India': President Donald Trump calls for lower interest rates in US to boost economic growth Trump-Xi summits give China 'strategic space' Xi broke with protocol to greet Trump at Shenzhen airport ahead of Thursday's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Trump called the gesture "a big win" even before his meetings began, similar to how he has described the pomp of previous meetings. Xi orchestrated moments befitting a visiting president focused on legacy-building: the pair shared a hug at the airport and held the first-ever trilateral meeting with Russia's Vladimir Putin. On substance, Xi was less generous. Trump told media outlets he and his Chinese counterpart had spoken about AI, trade and oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz. The US demands Beijing buy more US farm goods, ease curbs on rare-earth minerals vital to key industries and release two Americans who Washington says are wrongfully detained. China's Foreign Ministry said the two sides agreed to map out an action plan for building a "constructive relationship of strategic stability" — a framework already unveiled in May. The ministry gave no details or timeline. Beijing's readout did not mention the fragile US-China trade truce, China's agricultural commitments, rare earths, chip controls, the scandal over US chip giant Nvidia or the detained Americans, and did not name Iran. China is on track to meet its soybean pledge for 2026 but has delivered only a fraction of the other promised farm purchases, while rare-earth shipments remain far below the levels before the trade war escalated last year, and neither detained American has been freed. Xi also pushed his key demand that the US "keep doing the right thing" on Taiwan or risk setbacks in the bilateral relationship, according to the ministry. China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, a claim Taipei rejects. "China has secured additional strategic space, including the US stance on the Taiwan issue and the easing of the technology embargo. Strategically, the US has indeed gained nothing," said Dan Wang, China director at the Eurasia Group think tank. Trump's agenda focused heavily on the meeting with Xi and Putin, which released a joint "Declaration Toward Peace" that analysts described as vague. Hosting the trilateral summit, which Trump had pushed for, offered Xi a platform to cast himself as a central player in managing global affairs, analysts said. Abbas Araghchi says Iran wants diplomacy to end war; Trump says terms unacceptable China bides its time as US gets tougher on chips Since this month's resignation of Jensen Huang, a Trump ally, as Nvidia's CEO over the revelation that he had had an affair with a woman who US intelligence believes is a Chinese spy, the Trump administration has sought to close loopholes that let Chinese companies bypass US restrictions on AI chip exports. On the day Trump and Xi met, a US rule further restricting China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia took effect. The US administration is also weighing a rule requiring US companies to disclose their use of Chinese AI models. US lawmakers have also been moving against China. Beijing, which seeks to encourage Trump to stabilise bilateral relations while defending Chinese industries, has vowed retaliation against such curbs and is in no hurry to meet US demands, analysts say. "The Chinese see these noises as a natural part of the relationship," said Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese Foreign Ministry official who now works for Beijing-based think tank Global Governance Institution. "The Chinese have learned their lesson: they won't fulfil their side of a promise all at once. They'll do it step by step," he said. Holding back concessions gives Beijing leverage if Washington adopts a tougher stance, as pressure builds in Congress from lawmakers in both parties. This week, a House of Representatives committee report called for restricting investment in China's aerospace sector and a senator introduced legislation to revoke China's normal trade status and favourable tariff treatment. An extension of the trade truce is expected to wait until a meeting of Group of 20 leaders in Miami next month, when Xi and Trump are expected to meet again. The truce, struck at a meeting in South Korea last year and extended during Xi's visit to Washington in September, expires on January 10. The "low-hanging fruits have been harvested" after extensive trade talks over the past year, said Even Rogers Pay, director at Beijing-based consultancy Trivium China. "It may feel like a holding pattern by comparison to past summits, but in the current context it's actually a significant step, given the recent midterm elections and the Jensen Huang scandal." Analysts expect the year's fourth Trump-Xi meeting will also be heavy on optics. "But substantially, I don't think there's going to be very big progress. It's going to be about stability and stability," said Shen, the Chinese former official. "And that's enough."

UoH students launch protest seeking professor’s termination over casteist remarks
articles.summary: University of Hyderabad students have launched an indefinite protest demanding the termination of Dr Vijaya Ramdas Mandala, a faculty member in the History Department, over his alleged derogatory remarks about Dalit students in an email exchange. The remarks were allegedly made after a former student expressed hesitation regarding incorporating certain suggestions made by Vijaya Ramdas into his research because of ethical concerns. The incident took place in April but came to light only recently. The protest has been called by the Students’ Union, which comprises various student groups, including the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), the Ambedkar Students’ Association, the Dalit Students’ Union,and the Tribal Students’ Forum. Students have been staging a sit-in outside the Social Sciences building, demanding Vijaya Ramdas’s termination. “We will not call off the protest until Vijaya Ramdas is terminated,” Students’ Union general secretary Aditya Rao told TNM. “We had protested earlier too, but no concrete action was taken against him,” he added. The screenshots of an email exchange were shown to TNM by student activists. Through the emails, Vijaya Ramdas contacted Sandeep (name changed), who is a PhD student at Manchester Business School, about corrections to his chapter for a forthcoming book by Bloomsbury India. In the email thread, the History professor refers to former students from the Dalit community as “untouchables” more than once. He also refers to another student studying at Nottingham as “Dalit untouchable idiot”. The email exchange, which took place between April 14 and 16, grew increasingly tense after Sandeep said he would need the permission of his current university to anonymise the people he was being asked to name in the research, to avoid being flagged for ethical violations. “It will take months to get an ethical review committee's decision from the University of Manchester to write the names asked for in my chapter and publish it as a PhD student of the University,” Sandeep said. Vijaya Ramdas responded: “At Indian business schools, or even at Harvard Business School or Rotman Business School, your chapter discussing managerial and business people would not have been a problem. articles.title: Belonging: Sonia Gandhi’s memoir is from the heart, moving but playing it safe
articles.summary: The picture in your head, as you read Sonia Gandhi's Belonging , can at first be black and white and grainy like the front cover, of her young face looking at an India of nearly 60 years ago, when she first came here for love. The picture gathers colour as you read on and find Sonia at home in India, slowly and almost hesitatingly growing into the Congress veteran she has become. Just like in politics, she seems to have inadvertently captured her extraordinary life, without really wanting to, in her from-the-heart memoir. The book, selling like it had been awaited forever, though it was announced only earlier this year, may have that kind of pull because it comes from one of India’s most important political figures. But it is her writing that sustains that pull and keeps the reader turning the pages. When nonfiction has this kind of effect it is lazily lauded as reading like fiction. But Sonia’s life, overwhelmed with untoward incidents, could easily have become a chaotic mess on paper. One has to imagine that it is her artistic bent of mind (she writes about losing herself in museums) that brought order to the writing, placing in forefront the personal life that almost helplessly slips into the political. The way she begins makes you wonder if she simply dived into her past and picked up her first memory of Rajiv Gandhi and their meeting in an English cafe. She was 19, he 21, just bereaved of his grandfather Jawaharlal Nehru, the first Prime Minister of India. But Nehru and Indira Gandhi, Rajiv’s mother and yet another Prime Minister-to-be, do not come into the picture until later. Sonia keeps it personal for many pages, almost cheesily so, describing their days of courtship and her feelings for the young and handsome man, who at times, lost his temper. She details her childhood, growing up in fear of her disciplinarian dad, who can seem like an Amrish Puri of Indian Cinema, only he is in Orbassano of Italy, towering over his subdued wife and three daughters. Young Rajiv and Sonia It might be difficult to picture Sonia, the seasoned politician we have grown used to, as spending a regular middle class childhood in an Italian small town, and cowering in fear of her father. She waits too long to tell her parents about the relationship with Rajiv and when she does, predictably, all hell breaks loose. But in time, he allows her to visit India - to know the country as Rajiv insists Sonia should before planting her life there - only to be maddened by their hasty marriage. This is where you are introduced to the dominating presence of Indira Gandhi, the formidable mother-in-law that Sonia, subtle as she is with her words, manages to convey an image of. Sonia writes she was shocked by the suddenness of the wedding and pained by her father’s absence but nothing about what she did about it. You wonder if she questioned Rajiv, if she opposed it. Her timidness is something that she keeps worrying about, that would trouble her even in her later years of politics. It comes through in the unquestioning way she accepted that it would be she who made the move to a new country and adopt and adjust and not Rajiv. You don't even hear what she wanted to work as, her ambition or passion. The only time she lets herself whine is when she has to lose her family name, her last thread to where she came from. There is not the tone of reproach, and even at the places she admits being hurt by one in the family, she hastens to justify their actions or words. When the story shifts to life in India, the personal fades into the background and the political emerges. At first it is mere observation, learning of a new way of life, a new country, new people, and the governance of it. She makes no secret of having hated a life in politics and wanting no part of it for Rajiv or herself. She explodes when he decides to leave his beloved job of a pilot and plunges into politics as his brother Sanjay passes away. At several stages of her life, she looks back longingly at that old life, devoid of such fears and anxieties, and you wish for her that things had not gone the way they had and Rajiv had remained a pilot who loved photography. Priyanka, Rajiv, Sonia, Indira and Rahul with their dog Pippa in 1982 But even as she is honest about her feelings, she is cautiously curtailed in her descriptions of the family’s disastrous actions that would cost many lives and choke the democracy she sings praises about. One of India’s darkest times, the Emergency declared by Indira Gandhi, is written about like an objective piece of reporting, minus all the adjectives (viz. brutal) that she uses profusely when one of the family or members of the party are at the receiving end. Even as she tucks in a line or two about its horrors, it is a watered down version of the catastrophe. Her preceding passages even allow a line of justification for Indira, as not having an option, since that would destroy Congress and pave the way for the divisive forces of the RSS and the BJP. Almost naively Sonia does not question if Indira’s solution was to suspend democracy. Indira, who was so far presented as tough and unyielding, seems to crumble in the face of losing power and later, before her own flesh and blood, Sanjay Gandhi. Sonia is also disappointingly subdued in her writing of Sanjay Gandhi’s atrocities that brought so much havoc, including his forced vasectomies in the garb of family planning and the demolition at Turkman Gate. The only time she is liberal with her criticism of a family member is when she writes about Sanjay’s young wife Maneka Gandhi (who would later join the BJP). In Rajiv Gandhi’s case - the reluctant politician and Prime Minister - Sonia’s justifications of the scandals that scar his image appear to come from a genuine place of trust. But then she skims through the Bofors case, insisting on his innocence, without dwelling into the details. Even as she strongly condemns the anti-Sikh riots of 1984, she vehemently vouches for his 'just and compassionate ways' that would never allow him to authorise such heinous acts. She does not skip the controversies, including the Shah Bano case and the opening of the Babri Masjid for Hindu prayers, but gives a clean chit to her beloved every time. What Sonia calls her most cherished picture with Rajiv, taken by Priyanka Her fears about his life from the very first time he goes into politics melts your heart, and the inevitable death you know is coming only makes the description of the preceding days sad. It becomes all too relatable when she keeps blaming herself for not joining him for that last trip to Madras, after he had asked her to, in which he would be killed. Sonia could, more with sincere emotion than any technique of writing, have your heart racing as you read about her daughter Priyanka Gandhi knocking on her door urgently to pass on the news. She switches to the present tense to set the tragedy in real time, recounting the moment by moment shock of it. That she would fall and fall badly is a given. Sonia has unhesitatingly presented herself as a sensitive being, prone to tears, not bothering to project an iron-lady image in the ilk of her mother-in-law. She turns verbose in writing about the bond she holds with her children, Rahul who too enters politics after choosing another life, and Priyanka, who stands steadfastly behind her. Baby pictures of Rahul and Priyanka Even her decision to go into politics, a world she had wholeheartedly hated, seems to come more out of a sense of duty, because of her love and commitment and ways of obedience, than sheer will. But this does not portray her as a weak woman, only honest and unafraid to be so in this late telling of her story at the age of 80. Her strength in fact comes in these unrestrained but polite revelations. You have to shake your head when even in her passage about Narendra Modi, the BJP Prime Minister and political arch-enemy of the Congress, she tries to find a pattern, a reason for his ways. Not that she minces any words in her ‘polite’ criticism of the right wing or its many devastating actions and communal agenda. Sonia is clearly a leader who grew into her place, something that she wasn't naturally inclined to, but trained herself to. It begins from learning to love a new homeland she is planted to, amid so many towering personalities and tumultuous events, adapting with a lot of effort, picking a new language, absorbing a new culture and making India her own. Yet, after all that, she is most let down, not because she had to give up the Prime Ministerial post she’d won fair and square, but because she is still not recognised as one of us. If not for the 500 pages of her memoir, just her telling title can say so much about what has always been so close to her heart.
